Opening submissions by MR MUHYEALDEEN
MR MUHYEALDEEN:  Good morning, Mr Chairman and tribunal's
colleagues.  I will be conducting the opening
statement on behalf of the claimant.
Mr Chairman, members of the tribunal, colleagues,
good morning.
At the outset, please allow me to introduce
myself.  My name is Dr Naser Muhyealdeen from the law
offices of Hassan Al Riyami Advocates and Legal
Consultants.
I appear on behalf of the claimant Leaders Fort
Contracting LLC in this arbitration before the
Abu Dhabi International Arbitration Centre under case
number 2024-024.
I am joined today by my co-counsel, Mr Sary
Mohamed Badawi of Agile Project Management Advisors,
as well as our technical and quantum advisors from
Agile Project Management Advisors who have assisted
the claimant throughout these proceedings.
On behalf of the claimant and the entire legal
team, I would like to express our appreciation to the
tribunal for its time, attention and careful
consideration of the issues that arise in this
arbitration.
We are equally grateful to the secretariat and to
all those who involved in facilitating these
proceedings.
Mr Chairman, members of the tribunal, this morning
I propose to address the dispute in a manner that I
hope will be of assistance to the tribunal, rather
than beginning with individual claims deductions,
non-conformance reports referred to as NCRs, payment
certificates or experts calculations.  I intend to
start with the broader picture in our respectful
submissions unless one first understands the project
itself, the contractual relationship between the
parties and the circumstances in which this dispute
arose, it becomes very easy to lose sight of what this
case is actually about.
That observation is particularly important in the
present arbitration because the record before the
tribunal is substantial.  The parties have exchanged
extensive pleadings.  There are witness statements,
expert reports, project correspondence, inspection
records, payment applications, technical documents and
schedules.  As often happens in construction disputes,
the volume of material has a tendency to obscure
rather than illuminate the central issues.
For that reason, I would respectfully suggest that
the tribunal keep one question in mind throughout the
hearing: what is this dispute really about.  The
respondent's pleadings would have the tribunal believe
that this is a dispute concerning omissions,
incomplete facts, NCRs, open work inspection requests,
employer deductions and alleged overpayments.  Those
allegations occupy a considerable portion of the
respondent's case.
Indeed, by the time one reaches the end of the
respondent's submissions, one could be forgiven for
thinking that the claimant scarcely performed any
meaningful work at all.  The difficulty with the
narrative is that it bears little resemblance to the
reality of what occurred on the project.
The evidence will demonstrate that the claimant
was engaged as a specialist facade subcontractor for
The Pixel Project.  It mobilised its resources.  It
undertook engineering and design activities.  It
produced materials.  It fabricated components.  It
coordinated with other trades.  It installed
substantial portions of the facade package.  It
remained on the project over the extended period.  It
completed snagging and de-snagging works.  Ultimately,
the project received the benefit of the claimant's
performance.
The claimant performed substantial work.  The
respondent received the benefit of those work.  The
claimant remains unpaid for a significant portion of
the contract value and for the additional work carried
out during the course of the project.
The respondent's answer to that claim is not that
the work were never performed.  Rather, it answered
that -- his answer is that various deductions should
now be applied retrospectively so as to reduce,
extinguish or even reverse the claimant's
entitlements.  That, in essence, is a dispute which
the tribunal has been asked to determine.
Before examining those competing positions
however, it is necessary to return to the beginning
and consider how the relationship between the parties
developed, what the claimant was engaged to do, how
the project progressed, and why the parties ultimately
find themselves before this tribunal today.
The parties formalised the relationship throughout
subcontract agreement number HW-ADMD-ZY-070, which is
dated June 7, 2020.
Under that agreement, the claimant was entrusted
with a significant package of facade-related works.
Those responsibilities extended far beyond simple
installation activities.  They include design
obligations, engineering obligations, BIM
coordination, recruitment, fabrication, supply
delivery, installation, testing and commissioning.
In practical terms, the claimant was responsible
for taking a substantial portion of the facade package
from concept through to physical execution on site.
That distinction is important because throughout
these proceedings, the respondent has occasionally
sought to characterise the claimant's role in a narrow
fashion than the contractual documents themselves
support.  The reality is that the claimant was deeply
embedded within the delivery of this package.  Its
responsibilities touched almost every stage of the
process.  Engineering decisions had to be made,
materials had to be sourced, fabrication had to be
taking place, components had to be transported,
installation activities had to be coordinated with
numerous other trades operation across the projects.
The original subcontract value exceeded 7.7 million
dirhams.
Subsequently, the parties entered into amendment
number 1, increasing the subcontract value to
approximately 8.54 million dirham.  I mentioned that
amendments now, because it appears repeatedly
throughout the respondent's submissions.
In some respects, one gains the impression that
the respondent regards amendment number 1 as a
watershed moment that somehow altered the parties
right in a fundamental way.  With respect, it did not.
Amendment number 1 was exactly what its name
suggests; it was an amendment.  It was a commercial
adjustment made during the life of an ongoing project.
It reflected the reality that the project involved.
Scope evolves, commercial arrangements evolve, payment
mechanisms evolve.
Anyone who has spent time in the construction
industry understands that such amendments are not
unusual.  They are, in fact, commonplace.  The
respondent's treatment of amendment number 1
occasionally seems to lose sight of that principle.
We will return to that issue later in the hearing
because it becomes important when considering both the
final account and the variation claims.
For present purpose, it is sufficient to note that
the project continued, the subcontract continued, the
parties continued administering the works.  Payment
application continued, site activities continued.  The
commercial relationship remained very much alive.  And
that brings me to what was actually happening on the
ground.
Because one of the striking features of the
respondent's case is that it tends to examine
individual documents in isolation.  A particular NCR
is identified.  A particular WIR is identified.  A
particular comment is identified.  A particular
deduction is identified.  The implication is then
drawn that these documents somehow tell the story of
the project.  The claimant respectfully submits that
they do not.
The evidence will show that the claimant mobilised
its engineering resources and commenced performance.
It engaged suppliers.  It commenced recruitment
activities.  It undertook fabrication works.  It
coordinated with the respondent and with other trades'
operation on site.  It did precisely what one would
expect, especially subcontractor to do when asked, to
deliver a package of this manner.  At the same time,
however, the claimant was operating within a project
environment that was far from straightforward.
Now I should pause here because it's important
that the tribunal understands precisely why we raised
these issues.  The claimant is not pursuing a delay
claim.  The claimant is not asking this tribunal to
award prolongation costs.  The claimant is not seeking
compensation for every difficulty encountered during
execution.  This is not the case before you.  The
reason these matters are relevant is because they
provide the context with which the respondent's
allegation must be assessed.
The evidence will show repeated access
constraints.  It will show interference issues with
other trades.  It will show delay associated with
preceding works.  It will show ongoing coordinated
challenges.  None of these matters were unique to the
claimant.  They were project-wide realities.  They
formed part of the environment with which all
contractors and subcontractors were required to
operate.  Yet, despite those difficulties, the
claimant continued.  This is perhaps the most
important point at this stage of this case.
The claimant did not abandon the project.  Instead
it did what contractors are expected to do.  It
adapted, it coordinated, it addressed the issues as
they arose.  It continued progressing its work.  The
tribunal should therefore be cautious not to confuse
the existence of project administration documents with
evidence of nonperformance.  The two are not the same
thing.
Indeed, if one accepts the respondent's approach,
every NCR would become proof of defect works, every
open WIR would become proof of incomplete work and
every consultant comment would become proof of
contractual liability.
Construction projects do not operate in this
manner.  These documents are part of the
administration of the works.  They identify issues to
be addressed.  They do not determine the parties'
ultimate contractual rights.
What matters is where the project ultimately
arrived, and where the project ultimately arrived is
reflected in the progress record themselves.
The tribunal will hear evidence regarding interim
payments application number 14 -- a document of
particular significance in these proceedings.  By that
stage, the works were recorded as being approximately
97 per cent complete.
That figure reflects some reflection because it's
not a number created for the purpose of this
arbitration.  It's not the product of hindsight.  It
is not a figure generated by experts years later.  It
is a project record created during the execution of
the work themselves.
Now, a project that has reached approximately
97 per cent completion is not a project characterised
by wholesale nonperformance, nor is it a project in
which a subcontractor has failed to deliver the
essence of its contractual obligations.
On the contrary, it demonstrates that the
overwhelming majority of the subcontract work has been
carried out.  Therefore, the remaining snagging and
these snagging activities continued.
The evidence of the claimant will show that those
activities were completed by 9 February 2023.  By that
stage, the claimant has done what it has been engaged
to do.  It had performed the substantial works which
was required under the subcontract.  It had remained
engaged throughout the project lifecycle that it had
addressed.  Because if the claimant substantially
performed its obligation, if the project received the
benefits of those obligations, and if the works
ultimately progressed to completion, one is entitled
to ask a very simple question: what happened to the
money?
I ask that question deliberately, because
construction disputes often have a tendency to become
unnecessarily complicated.  Figures multiply,
spreadsheets become larger, deductions are layered
upon deductions.  Entire debates emerge concerning
administrative record, approval procedures and
internal valuations.  After a while, one risks losing
sight of the basic commercial bargain that brought the
parties together in the first place.
The tribunal will hear extensive evidence
regarding the final accounts, but it's important not
to allow the mechanics of the final account process to
obscure the underlying reality.
The claimant is not advancing a claim for
hypothetical works.  It's not advancing a claim based
upon future opportunities.  It's not claiming for
works it intended to perform but never performed.  The
claim concerns work that was actually carried out,
resources that were actually deployed, and the value
that was actually delivered to the project.  The first
component concerns the local sealed package.
Now, one can describe the local sealed package in
various ways.  One can refer to quantities.  One can
refer to fabrication records.  One can refer to
recruitment schedules.  One can refer to engineering
drawings.  Ultimately, however, the significance of
this package lies in something much simpler.  It
performed part of the physical works required for
successful execution of the facade system.  It was not
theoretical.  It was not optional.  It was not
something that existed only on paper.  The steel had
to be engineered.  The steel had to be procured.  The
steel had to be fabricated.  The steel had to be
delivered, and substantial portions of the steelworks
had to be installed.
Those activities require manpower.  They require
expertise.  They require expenditures.  They require
commitment on the part of the claimants.  They
required commitment on the part of the claimant.
The tribunal will see from the evidence that these
were not activities carried out in anticipation of
some future entitlements.  They were carried out
because the subcontract required them and because the
project needed them.
Yet, despite all that, the amount of 747,059
dirhams remains outstanding now.
What is striking about the respondent's position
is that it does not seriously contend that these
activities never occurred.  The respondent does not
suggest that the steel was never procured.
Instead, the respondent seeks to arrive at the
same destination through a different route.  It sees
that the deduction should be applied.  It says that
certain matters remain unresolved.  It says that
various issues identified elsewhere in the project
justify withholding the payment.
The respondent's case frequently skips over those
intermediate steps.  The same pattern emerges in
relation to the installation works.
The outstanding sum claimed by the claimant in
respect of installation activities amount to 733,625
dirhams.
Again, this is not a claim detached from reality.
It arises from installation works that formed part of
the claimant's contractual obligation and which
contributed directly to the completed project.
The tribunal will hear evidence concerning the
extent of those activities, the resources committed to
them and the manner in which they were executed
throughout the course of the project.
Therefore, the tribunal is left with a fundamental
question: on what basis can payment for those works
properly be withheld?
That question becomes even more significant when
one turns to the issue of variations, because the
variation claims reveal something important about the
way this project was actually executed.  They reveal
that the claimant was not operating with a static
environment where they were drawing, every detail,
every requirement remained fixed from the beginning to
the end.
Now, I do not intend, at this stage, to take the
tribunal through each variation claim individually.
There will be an appropriate opportunity to do so
later in this proceedings when we examine the
documentary record, the witness evidence and the
expert analysis in greater detail.
For present purposes, however, it is important to
understand the broader context in which these claims
arose.
Construction projects are dynamic undertaking.
They do not proceed from commencement to completion in
precisely the same form as originally envisaged.
Designs evolve, interfaces develop, site conditions
present challenges that were not apparent to tender
stage, employers introduce changes, consultants revise
requirements, contractors are required to adapt.  That
is not an indication that something has gone wrong.
It is often simply the reality of delivering a complex
construction project.
As the evidence will show, the claimant was
required to undertake additional work arising from the
design, development, engineering requirements and
modification affecting elements of the steel packages
and related works.
These were not works that appeared for the first
time in the context of this arbitration, nor are they
claims manufactured with the benefits of hindsight.
Those arose during the life of the project itself and
were direct consequences of the way in which the
project developed.
The dispute before the tribunal is therefore not
whether these additional activities occurred, nor is
it whether the project changed over time.  The
documentary record demonstrates that it did.
The real dispute concerns the consequences of
these changes, and whether the claimant should be
fairly compensated for work that fell outside the
scope originally contemplated by the parties.
We will return to those variation claims in due
course.  At that stage, the tribunal will hear
detailed evidence concerning the nature of the
changes, the circumstances in which they arose and the
contractual basis upon which the claimant advances its
entitlement.
For the moment, however, it is sufficient to
observe that the variation claims form part of the
broader picture that emerges repeatedly throughout
this arbitration.  The claimant was not standing
still.  The project was not standing still.  The
parties were dealing with the project that continued
to evolve and the claimant continued to respond to
those developments in order to ensure that the works
progressed.
It is against the background that one must
consider the respondent's defence and in particular,
the counterclaim advanced in these proceedings,
because once one accepts the substantial works were
performed and that the project progressed, and the
claimant remained engaged throughout execution, and
that additional work was undertaken as the project
evolved, the tribunal is driven to ask for the
question: on what basis does the respondent say that
none of this is payable?
It is to that question that I now turn.  It is
worth pausing at this point because the respondent
defence occupies a significant portion of these
proceedings, and in fairness to the respondent, it
deserves careful consideration.
The claimant position is not that the respondent
is prevented from raising complaints, nor it is the
claimant's position that the deduction can never be
made under a construction contract.  Construction
projects are complex, disputes arise, defects occur,
works are sometimes limited.  Contractors and
subcontractors frequently disagree regarding
responsibility.  None of that is controversial.
The difficulty, however, lays in the manner in
which the respondent seeks to advance its case.  When
one examines respondent defence closely, one begins to
notice a recurring pattern.  A particular issue is
identified.  That issue is then assigned a financial
consequence.  The financial consequence is then
treated as an established deduction.  The deduction is
then carried forward into the final account.  By the
end of the exercise what began as an allegation has
effectively become a proven liability.  This point may
appear obvious, but it is fundamental to the tribunal
task.
The tribunal is not being asked whether concerns
were raised during the project.  Plainly they were.
The tribunal is not being asked whether inspection
generated comments.  Plainly they did.  The tribunal
is not being asked whether disagreement arose during
execution.  Again, plainly they did.
The tribunal is being asked something much more
specific.  The tribunal is being asked whether the
respondent has established a contractual basis for
withholding payments and, further, whether it
established an entitlement to recover monies from the
claimant by way of counterclaim.  The respondent's
case relies heavily upon documents such as NCR and
WIR, consultants comments and employer deductions.
One encountered these documents repeatedly
throughout the pleadings and expert reports.  The
implication is often that the existence of such
document is itself evidence of liability.
The claimant respectfully submits that it is not.
Taking nonconformance report as an example, an NCR at
its highest records that a concern has been
identified.  It is part of the project administration
process.  It is a tool used to identify issues
required in an investigation, clarification or
corrective action.
It is not a finding of liability.  It is not a
judicial determination.  It does not establish
causation.  It does not establish loss.  It certainly
does not establish that a party is entitled to recover
a particular sum of money.
Yet, one repeatedly encounters the suggestion that
because an NCR existed, liability somehow follows
automatically.
The same difficulty arises with respect to WIR.  A
work inspection request is precisely what its name
suggests.  It is part of an inspection process.  It
records inspection requested, inspections undertaken
and comments made during the course of project
execution.
It does not determine contractual responsibility.
It does not determine whether work was ultimately
completed.  It does not determine whether a deduction
is justified.
If the existence of an NCR were sufficient to
establish liability, every contractor on every major
project would be liable for substantial deduction.  If
the existence of an open WIR were sufficient to
establish nonperformance, very few projects would ever
reach completion.  That is not how construction
projects operate.
The tribunal must look beyond the existence of the
documents and examine what the document actually
proves.  And when the exercise is undertaken, one
encounters a recurring difficulty in respondent's
case.  The respondent frequently identifies the
document, what is often missing is the next step.
What precisely was the consequence?  What loss was
suffered?  Who suffered it?  And how was that loss
calculated?  What evidence supports the calculations?
Why is the claimant contractually responsible for it?
Those questions become particularly important when
one turns to the employer deduction upon which the
respondent places considerable reliance.  The
respondent must still establish why the deductions
arose, how it relates to the claimant's scope, whether
the claimant was responsible for the underlying
issues, and whether the amount claimed accurately
reflects any loss allegedly attributable to the
claimant.
That, in our respectful submission, is where the
respondent's case begins to encounter significant
difficulty, because once one moves beyond the labels
and begins examining the underlying evidence, the
counterclaim starts to look far less certain than the
respondent would suggest.
Indeed, the tribunal will see that many of the
deductions ultimately depend upon propositions that
are either unsupported by evidence, disconnected from
any demonstrable loss, or incapable of establishing
the causal link required to impose liability upon the
claimant.
It is therefore necessary to examine those
deductions individually and to consider whether they
can withstand scrutiny when measured against the
contractual framework and the evidence before the
tribunal.
It is those specific allegations that I now turn.
The respondent's first category of deduction
concerns the alleged omissions of ground floor
